claims.text: The initial material is as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C and strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr has poor oxygen resistance.
A thin, dense anti-oxidation coating will significantly improve the alloy's high-temperature oxygen resistance.
Applying the coating will not degrade room-temperature tensile ductility.
Applying the coating will not degrade elevated-temperature yield strength.
An alumina-based or similar oxide coating can be deposited by thermal spraying or chemical vapor deposition.
The proposed evaluation condition is approximately 1000 °C in air for 100 hours.
The coating will form a continuous, stable oxide scale on the alloy surface.
The continuous oxide scale will act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion into HfNbTaTiZr.
Chemical and thermal stability of the protective oxide layer at high temperature will prevent oxygen ingress.
Preventing oxygen ingress will preserve the underlying alloy microstructure.
Preservation of the underlying microstructure will preserve the alloy's mechanical properties.
Relative to the uncoated alloy, the coated alloy will have reduced oxidation weight gain.
Relative to the uncoated alloy, the coated alloy will have reduced surface degradation.
The intervention is expected to remain effective during steady-state high-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere.
Performance under cyclic thermal shock and extreme mechanical fatigue has not been established.
Long-term coating adhesion and stability under cyclic thermal loading and severe deformation are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The conditions field suggests that samples are mechanically loaded at specified strain rates while undergoing the 100-hour oxidation exposure, whereas the experiment describes oxidation exposure followed by separate tensile tests. These represent different thermomechanical histories.
